abstract: Background: Rapid urbanization in Brazil has shifted the epidemiological landscape of parasitic diseases, such as schistosomiasis and malaria. Although typically considered a rural infection, Schistosoma mansoni transmission persists in urban settings where sanitation and water access remain uneven. This study investigates the persistence and dynamics of urban schistosomiasis across neighborhoods of Salvador, Bahia, Brazil. Methods: Between 2011 and 2024 cross-sectional surveys were conducted to identify neighborhoods with the highest prevalence in the major metropolitan area of Salvador, Bahia. A total of 6,863 residents provided demographic information and Kato-Katz examination of at least one stool sample. We conducted demographic surveys and stool examination on 3,964 individuals who were re-examined on up to three occasions at intervals ranging from 1-5 years. Findings: The overall prevalence of initial examination was 7%. Regardless of treatment intervals, the community-wide prevalence declined by more than half and did not rebound. Apparent Incidence decreased to <0.5%/year following a second period of treatment. In nearly all communities, most infections occurred among individuals born in Salvador with no travel history outside the city. Interpretation: Overall, the study provides one of the first individual-level longitudinal assessments of schistosomiasis persistence in an urban Brazilian setting, combining repeated parasitological surveys with demographic and environmental data across multiple neighborhoods. These findings indicate that schistosomiasis transmission in Salvador is largely local rather than imported. The decline in prevalence coincides with observed community-level improvements in sanitation and reduced contact with surface water. f prevalence rates were applied across the population of Salvador, this city could be considered one of the state’s most important endemic areas. Author summary: Rapid urbanization and the lack of accompanying sanitation is urbanizing diseases previously considered rural. While sanitation in Salvador is generally good, Schistosoma mansoni infection was identified in all poor neighborhoods examined, and most evidence indicates this is a result of active transmission. Studies in urban environments pose difficulties not experienced or experienced to a lesser degree in most rural areas. Participation in research is lower, and violence is generally higher. Urban areas also offer opportunities for effective intervention due to the greater impact of infrastructure modifications and population density. Interventions tend to more easily affect a greater number of people. The prevalence of infection and the size of the city make urban infection an important focus for management. The Brazilian setting may provide a preview of schistosomiasis transmission as endemic areas become increasingly urbanized.
docs.title_display: Schistosomiasis as an urban disease: 13 years of studies in the neighborhoods of Salvador, BA, Brazil

abstract: Background: Massive bee stings can cause systemic manifestations and life-threatening complications. In French Guiana, data on such envenomations are scarce. This study aimed to describe the epidemiology, clinical characteristics, and management of patients presenting to the emergency department. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed medical records of all patients admitted for bee stings over the period 2014–2023 at Cayenne Hospital. A composite variable of systemic involvement was created (neurological, respiratory, hemodynamic and digestive). All analyses were descriptive. An exploratory two-graph receiver operating characteristic (TG-ROC) analysis was used to describe the sensitivity and specificity of sting-count cut-offs for four binary indicators of systemic involvement. Results: Among 143 patients included, 40% (n = 57) presented at least one systemic manifestation. The median number of stings was 50 [20–150]. In the exploratory TG-ROC analysis, the cut-offs maximizing the Youden index were approximately 72 stings for digestive and hemodynamic manifestations and 99 stings for neurological and respiratory manifestations, with modest sensitivity (0.50–0.76) and specificity (0.68–0.76). Overall mortality was low (0.7%, n = 1/143). Conclusions: This study provides the first detailed epidemiological and clinical description of massive bee envenomations in French Guiana. Exploratory analyses suggested that systemic manifestations may occur at sting counts below the conventional 200-sting threshold. These findings should not be interpreted as a validated clinical cutoff and require confirmation in prospective multicenter studies. Author summary: Most bee stings cause only local pain and swelling. However, being stung many times can lead to serious illness because of the large amount of venom injected. Few studies have described these multiple-sting attacks in French Guiana. We reviewed the medical records of 143 patients treated at Cayenne Hospital after multiple honey bee stings between 2014 and 2023. Most patients were men, and the median number of stings was 50. Forty percent of patients developed at least one systemic manifestation, such as breathing problems, low blood pressure, severe digestive symptoms, or neurological symptoms. Our results suggest that such symptoms may occur after fewer than the 200 stings traditionally considered to indicate severe envenomation. However, this observation needs to be confirmed, as our study was retrospective and based on patients treated at a single hospital, and the number of stings was estimated from medical records. These findings suggest that people who have been stung many times should be assessed carefully, even when the number of stings is below 200. Further studies are needed to confirm these results.
docs.title_display: Massive envenomations by bees in French Guiana: A ten-year retrospective study (2014–2023)
